docs.title: Microeconomics: An Intelligent Textbook
docs.text:
Prof. Sharat Batra · University of Minnesota · batra052@umn.edu

Welcome to Microeconomics: An Intelligent Textbook — an open, interactive course resource designed for undergraduate students at the University of Minnesota and beyond.

This textbook covers the core principles of microeconomics through clear explanations, real-world examples, mathematical models, and interactive simulations. Each chapter builds on the last, taking you from the foundational ideas of scarcity and choice all the way to international trade and behavioral economics.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• How individuals and firms make decisions under scarcity
  • How markets coordinate supply and demand to set prices
  • How different market structures (competition, monopoly, oligopoly) affect outcomes
  • How markets can fail and what policy can do about it
  • How insights from psychology reshape our understanding of economic behavior

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
This course introduces the fundamental principles of microeconomics — the study of how individuals, households, and firms make decisions in the face of scarcity, and how these decisions interact through markets. Students will develop analytical tools to understand resource allocation, price determination, market structure, and government policy.

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • Apply the core economic concepts of scarcity, opportunity cost, and marginal analysis
  • Model supply, demand, and market equilibrium graphically and mathematically
  • Analyze how different market structures affect prices, output, and social welfare
  • Evaluate the causes and consequences of market failures
  • Apply microeconomic reasoning to real-world policy questions

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Define economics and distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics
  2. Explain scarcity, choice, and the concept of opportunity cost
  3. Apply marginal analysis to decision-making
  4. Construct and interpret a Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
  5. Identify the role of incentives and trade in economic reasoning

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Economics?
docs.text:
Economics is the study of how individuals, firms, and societies allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants. Because resources — time, money, land, labor — are limited, every economic agent must make choices. Economics provides the tools to analyze those choices systematically.

Two Branches of Economics

  • Microeconomics studies individual decision-makers: households, firms, and specific markets. Why does coffee cost more than water? Why do nurses earn less than surgeons?
  • Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: total output, unemployment, inflation, and economic growth. Why did GDP fall during COVID-19? What causes inflation?

This textbook focuses on microeconomics.

docs.title: The Fundamental Problem
docs.text:
Scarcity means that resources are limited relative to human wants. This is the central fact of economic life. Because we cannot have everything, we must choose. Every choice involves a trade-off — getting more of one thing means getting less of another.

Scarcity in everyday life

You have 24 hours in a day. If you spend 3 hours studying economics, those 3 hours cannot also be spent sleeping, working, or watching TV. Time is scarce; you must allocate it.

docs.title: Opportunity Cost
docs.text:
The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up when you make that choice. It is the true cost of any decision.

\[\text{Opportunity Cost} = \text{Value of the Next-Best Alternative Foregone}\]

Opportunity cost of college

The full cost of attending college is not just tuition and books. It also includes the foregone wages you could have earned by working instead. For a student who could earn $35,000/year, the opportunity cost of a four-year degree includes $140,000 in foregone income — even if tuition is free.

Key insight: Opportunity costs are often hidden. Economists think about all costs — not just the ones that show up on a bill.

docs.title: Sunk Costs
docs.text:
A sunk cost is a cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered. Rational decision-making requires ignoring sunk costs and focusing only on future costs and benefits.

The sunk cost fallacy

You bought a $15 movie ticket but the film is terrible. Should you stay to "get your money's worth"? No — the $15 is gone regardless. The only relevant question is: Will the next two hours of my life be better spent watching this movie or doing something else?

docs.title: 1.3 Marginal Analysis
docs.text:
Economists think at the margin. A marginal change is a small, incremental change. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefits of an action to its additional costs.

The Rule: Pursue an activity as long as the marginal benefit (MB) exceeds or equals the marginal cost (MC).

\[\text{Optimal choice: MB} = \text{MC}\]

docs.title: Example: How many hours to study?
docs.text:
Suppose each additional hour of studying raises your exam grade, but with diminishing returns:

Study Hours Marginal Benefit (grade points gained) Marginal Cost (value of time foregone) 1st hour 20 5 2nd hour 15 5 3rd hour 10 5 4th hour 5 5 5th hour 2 5

The optimal choice is 4 hours — where MB = MC = 5. Studying a 5th hour costs more than it's worth.

Marginal thinking in business

An airline has a flight from Minneapolis to Chicago that is half-full. Should it sell the remaining seats at a discount? Yes — as long as the discounted fare exceeds the marginal cost of adding a passenger (essentially zero for an already-flying plane). The fixed costs of the flight are sunk.

docs.title: Diminishing Marginal Returns
docs.text:
As you do more of something, holding everything else constant, the marginal benefit typically falls. This is the principle of diminishing marginal returns (or diminishing marginal utility for consumers).

  • The first slice of pizza is wonderful. The fifth is less enjoyable.
  • The first hour of studying helps a lot. The tenth hour adds little.

docs.title: 1.4 The Production Possibilities Frontier
docs.text: The Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) is a model that illustrates the trade-offs facing an economy (or individual) that produces two goods using fixed resources.

docs.title: Constructing the PPF
docs.text:
Consider a small economy that can produce only wheat and computers, using all available labor and capital.

Production Possibility Wheat (millions of bushels) Computers (millions of units) A 0 30 B 5 27 C 10 21 D 15 12 E 18 0

Plotting these combinations traces the PPF — a curve bowing outward from the axes.

docs.title: Key Features of the PPF
docs.text:
1. Points on the curve — efficient: all resources are fully employed.

2. Points inside the curve — inefficient: resources are idle or wasted (e.g., during a recession).

3. Points outside the curve — currently unattainable with existing resources and technology.

4. The slope of the PPF = the opportunity cost of producing one more unit of a good.

docs.title: Why Is the PPF Bowed Outward?
docs.text:
The outward bow (concave shape) reflects the law of increasing opportunity costs: as you produce more of one good, you must give up increasing amounts of the other. This happens because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods — the most productive wheat farmers are moved to computer production last.

\[\text{Opportunity Cost of Computers} = \frac{\Delta \text{Wheat}}{\Delta \text{Computers}}\]

As we move from A to E (producing more wheat), the opportunity cost of each additional bushel of wheat rises.

docs.title: Shifts in the PPF
docs.text:
The PPF shifts outward when:

  • More resources are available (e.g., population growth, capital investment)
  • Technology improves (higher productivity for one or both goods)

Technological progress

If a new variety of wheat doubles agricultural productivity, the PPF shifts outward along the wheat axis — the economy can now produce more wheat without sacrificing any computers.

docs.title: Comparative Advantage and Specialization
docs.text: Two individuals (or countries) can both gain by specializing in the good for which they have the lower opportunity cost and then trading. This is the principle of comparative advantage (covered in depth in Chapter 16).

docs.title: 1.5 Economic Models and Assumptions
docs.text:
Economists build models — simplified representations of reality — to isolate and study specific relationships. A model deliberately ignores some details to focus on what matters most.

Common economic assumptions:

  • Ceteris paribus ("all else equal") — when analyzing one variable, hold others constant
  • Rational behavior — individuals make choices to maximize their well-being given constraints
  • Equilibrium — markets tend toward a state where supply equals demand

Models are not perfect — they are useful

A map of Minneapolis that showed every building, tree, and pothole would be unusable. A useful map simplifies. Economic models do the same thing: they sacrifice realism for insight.

docs.title: Positive vs. Normative Economics
docs.text:
Positive Normative Nature Descriptive — what is Prescriptive — what ought to be Example "A minimum wage increase reduces employment for low-skill workers." "The minimum wage should be raised to $15/hour." Verifiable? In principle, yes No — depends on values

Economists try to keep these separate. A positive analysis of the minimum wage does not tell you whether to support it; that depends on your values and how you weigh trade-offs.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Scarcity The condition in which resources are limited relative to wants Opportunity Cost The value of the next-best alternative foregone Sunk Cost A past cost that cannot be recovered and should be ignored Marginal Analysis Decision-making by comparing marginal benefits to marginal costs Marginal Benefit (MB) The additional benefit from one more unit of an activity Marginal Cost (MC) The additional cost from one more unit of an activity Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce Efficiency Producing at a point on the PPF (no waste) Law of Increasing Opportunity Costs As more of a good is produced, its opportunity cost rises Comparative Advantage The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer Ceteris Paribus Latin for "all else equal" — a modeling assumption Positive Economics Analysis of what is (factual, testable) Normative Economics Analysis of what ought to be (value-based)

docs.title: Problem 1 — Opportunity Cost
docs.text:
Maria is a dentist who earns $150/hour. She decides to spend a Saturday afternoon (4 hours) painting her living room rather than hiring a painter who charges $40/hour.

a) What is the explicit cost of painting the room herself? b) What is the opportunity cost of painting the room herself? c) From an economic standpoint, is it rational for Maria to paint the room herself?

Solution

a) The explicit cost is $0 — she is not paying anyone.

b) The opportunity cost is the foregone dentist income: 4 hours × $150/hour = $600.

c) The total economic cost of Maria painting is $600 (opportunity cost) compared to $160 (paying the painter). It is not rational from a purely economic standpoint — she should hire the painter and spend those 4 hours working as a dentist.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Sunk Cost
docs.text:
You paid $80 for a non-refundable ticket to a concert. On the day of the concert, you feel slightly ill and estimate that attending will give you $30 of enjoyment, while staying home and resting will give you $60 of enjoyment.

a) Should you attend the concert? Why or why not? b) Does the $80 ticket price affect your decision?

Solution

a) You should stay home. The relevant comparison is: $30 (attending) vs. $60 (resting). Resting gives you more utility.

b) No. The $80 is a sunk cost — it is gone regardless of what you do. Rational decision-making ignores sunk costs.

docs.title: Problem 3 — Marginal Analysis
docs.text:
A firm's data on weekly output is shown below:

Workers Total Output (units) Marginal Product Marginal Revenue ($10/unit) Marginal Labor Cost ($200/worker) 1 50 50 $500 $200 2 95 45 $450 $200 3 130 35 $350 $200 4 155 25 $250 $200 5 170 15 $150 $200 6 180 10 $100 $200

a) How many workers should the firm hire? b) What principle guides this decision?

Solution

a) The firm should hire 4 workers. At 4 workers, the marginal revenue product ($250) still exceeds the marginal cost ($200). Adding a 5th worker costs $200 but generates only $150 in revenue — a net loss.

b) The MB = MC principle: hire as long as the marginal benefit (marginal revenue product) exceeds the marginal cost (wage).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Production Possibilities Frontier
docs.text:
An economy produces only food and clothing. With all resources devoted to food, it can produce 120 units. With all resources devoted to clothing, it can produce 60 units. Assume the PPF is a straight line.

a) Draw the PPF and label the intercepts. b) What is the opportunity cost of 1 unit of clothing in terms of food? c) What is the opportunity cost of 1 unit of food in terms of clothing? d) If the economy is producing at (60 food, 30 clothing), is it efficient?

Solution

a) The PPF runs from (0 food, 60 clothing) to (120 food, 0 clothing) — a straight line.

b) Opportunity cost of 1 unit of clothing = 120/60 = 2 units of food.

c) Opportunity cost of 1 unit of food = 60/120 = 0.5 units of clothing.

d) The point (60, 30) lies exactly on the PPF (it satisfies the constraint: 60/120 + 30/60 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1). This is an efficient point.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Positive vs. Normative
docs.text:
Classify each statement as positive or normative.

  1. "The United States spends about 18% of GDP on healthcare."
  2. "The government should provide universal healthcare."
  3. "Rent control reduces the quantity of housing supplied."
  4. "Housing is a human right and should not be subject to market prices."
Solution
  1. Positive — a factual, measurable claim.
  2. Normative — a value judgment about policy.
  3. Positive — a testable prediction of economic theory.
  4. Normative — a statement about values, not facts.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 2: Supply and Demand, we use these foundations to build the most powerful tool in economics — the supply-and-demand model.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Explain the law of demand and construct a demand curve
  2. Explain the law of supply and construct a supply curve
  3. Identify the determinants that shift supply and demand curves
  4. Find the market equilibrium price and quantity
  5. Analyze how supply and demand shifts change equilibrium
  6. Explain the concepts of consumer surplus, producer surplus, and market efficiency

docs.title: 2.1 Markets
docs.text:
A market is any arrangement that facilitates the exchange of a good or service between buyers and sellers. Markets can be physical (a farmers' market), virtual (Amazon), or decentralized (the labor market). The price that emerges in a market coordinates the decisions of buyers and sellers without any central authority directing them.

Markets everywhere

  • The market for Minneapolis apartment rentals
  • The market for computer science graduates
  • The New York Stock Exchange
  • The global market for crude oil

docs.title: The Law of Demand
docs.text:
Demand refers to the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity that consumers are willing and able to buy, holding all else equal.

The Law of Demand: When the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls (and vice versa), ceteris paribus.

\[Q_d = f(P, \overline{I}, \overline{P_r}, \overline{\text{Tastes}}, \overline{E}, \overline{N})\]

where \(P\) is price (variable) and the bars denote factors held constant.

The demand curve is a downward-sloping line (or curve) showing the quantity demanded at each price.

docs.title: Why Does Demand Slope Downward?
docs.text:
Two effects explain the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded:

  1. Substitution effect: When the price of coffee rises, consumers substitute toward tea. The good becomes relatively more expensive.
  2. Income effect: When the price of coffee rises, consumers' purchasing power falls — they can afford less of everything, including coffee.

docs.title: The Demand Schedule and Curve
docs.text:
Consider the market for gasoline in Minneapolis:

Price ($/gallon) Quantity Demanded (million gallons/month) $2.00 60 $3.00 50 $4.00 40 $5.00 30 $6.00 20

Plotting price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis gives a downward-sloping demand curve.

docs.title: Movements Along vs. Shifts of the Demand Curve
docs.text:
Movement along the demand curve: Caused only by a change in the price of the good itself. This is a change in quantity demanded.

Shift of the demand curve: Caused by a change in any other factor that affects demand. The entire curve moves left (decrease) or right (increase).

docs.title: Determinants of Demand (Demand Shifters)
docs.text:
Determinant Increase in Demand Decrease in Demand Income (normal good) Income rises Income falls Income (inferior good) Income falls Income rises Price of a substitute Substitute price rises Substitute price falls Price of a complement Complement price falls Complement price rises Consumer tastes Good becomes more popular Good becomes less popular Expectations (future price ↑) Buy more now Buy less now Number of buyers More buyers Fewer buyers

Substitutes and complements

  • Substitutes: Butter and margarine. If the price of butter rises, demand for margarine increases (the demand curve for margarine shifts right).
  • Complements: Cars and gasoline. If the price of gasoline rises, demand for large cars decreases (the demand curve for large cars shifts left).

Normal vs. inferior goods

  • Normal goods: As income rises, demand rises. Example: restaurant meals, new cars.
  • Inferior goods: As income rises, demand falls. Example: instant noodles, used cars. (People switch to better substitutes when they can afford it.)

docs.title: The Law of Supply
docs.text:
Supply refers to the relationship between the price of a good and the quantity that producers are willing and able to sell, holding all else equal.

The Law of Supply: When the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises (and vice versa), ceteris paribus.

The supply curve is an upward-sloping line (or curve) showing the quantity supplied at each price.

docs.title: Why Does Supply Slope Upward?
docs.text:
• Higher prices make production more profitable, inducing existing firms to expand output and attracting new firms into the market.
  • At higher prices, firms are willing to incur higher marginal costs to supply more units.

docs.title: The Supply Schedule and Curve
docs.text: Price ($/gallon) Quantity Supplied (million gallons/month) $2.00 20 $3.00 30 $4.00 40 $5.00 50 $6.00 60

docs.title: Determinants of Supply (Supply Shifters)
docs.text:
Determinant Increase in Supply Decrease in Supply Input prices (e.g., wages, materials) Input costs fall Input costs rise Technology Productivity improves Productivity falls Number of sellers More sellers enter Sellers exit Government policy Subsidy given Tax imposed Expectations (future price ↑) Withhold supply now — Prices of related goods in production Alternative good price falls Alternative good price rises

Technology and supply

The development of hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") dramatically lowered the cost of extracting natural gas. This shifted the supply curve for natural gas rightward — producers were willing to supply more at every price, driving down the market price.

docs.title: Finding Equilibrium
docs.text:
Market equilibrium occurs where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. At the equilibrium price (\(P^*\)), the market clears — there is no unsatisfied demand and no unsold surplus.

\[Q_d(P^*) = Q_s(P^*) \implies \text{market equilibrium}\]

Using our gasoline example:

Price \(Q_d\) \(Q_s\) Surplus / Shortage $2.00 60 20 Shortage of 40 $3.00 50 30 Shortage of 20 $4.00 40 40 Equilibrium $5.00 30 50 Surplus of 20 $6.00 20 60 Surplus of 40

The equilibrium is \(P^* = \$4.00\), \(Q^* = 40\) million gallons.

docs.title: Surplus and Shortage
docs.text:
Surplus (excess supply): When price is above equilibrium, \(Q_s > Q_d\). Unsold goods accumulate; sellers lower prices. The market self-corrects downward toward \(P^*\).

Shortage (excess demand): When price is below equilibrium, \(Q_d > Q_s\). Buyers compete for scarce goods; prices are bid up. The market self-corrects upward toward \(P^*\).

The market as a coordinating mechanism

Prices serve as signals. A price above equilibrium signals "too much supply — cut back." A price below equilibrium signals "too much demand — produce more." No central planner is needed.

docs.title: Mathematical Example
docs.text:
Suppose the demand and supply equations for a good are:

\[Q_d = 100 - 2P$$ $$Q_s = 10 + 3P\]

Finding equilibrium:

\[Q_d = Q_s$$ $$100 - 2P = 10 + 3P$$ $$90 = 5P$$ $$P^* = 18$$ $$Q^* = 100 - 2(18) = 64\]

The equilibrium price is $18 and equilibrium quantity is 64 units.

docs.title: 2.5 Changes in Equilibrium
docs.text:
When supply or demand shifts, the equilibrium changes. Use the following three-step method:

Step 1: Draw the initial supply and demand curves and mark the initial equilibrium. Step 2: Determine which curve shifts, and in which direction. Step 3: Find the new equilibrium and describe what happened to \(P\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Case 1: Demand Increases
docs.text:
Example: A hot summer increases demand for ice cream.

  • Demand curve shifts right.
  • At the old price, there is a shortage.
  • Price is bid up → equilibrium price rises.
  • Higher price induces more production → equilibrium quantity rises.

Result: Both P and Q rise.

docs.title: Case 2: Demand Decreases
docs.text:
Example: A health study links red meat to cancer, reducing beef demand.

  • Demand curve shifts left.
  • At the old price, there is a surplus.
  • Price falls → equilibrium price falls.
  • Lower price reduces production → equilibrium quantity falls.

Result: Both P and Q fall.

docs.title: Case 3: Supply Increases
docs.text:
Example: Better corn seed technology increases corn supply.

  • Supply curve shifts right.
  • At the old price, there is a surplus.
  • Price falls → equilibrium price falls.
  • Lower price increases quantity demanded → equilibrium quantity rises.

Result: P falls, Q rises.

docs.title: Case 4: Supply Decreases
docs.text:
Example: A drought destroys part of the wheat crop.

  • Supply curve shifts left.
  • At the old price, there is a shortage.
  • Price rises → equilibrium price rises.
  • Higher price reduces quantity demanded → equilibrium quantity falls.

Result: P rises, Q falls.

docs.title: Summary of Equilibrium Effects
docs.text:
Event Demand Supply \(\Delta P^*\) \(\Delta Q^*\) Demand increases Shifts right Unchanged ↑ ↑ Demand decreases Shifts left Unchanged ↓ ↓ Supply increases Unchanged Shifts right ↓ ↑ Supply decreases Unchanged Shifts left ↑ ↓ Both increase Shifts right Shifts right ? ↑↑ Demand ↑, Supply ↓ Shifts right Shifts left ↑↑ ?

Simultaneous shifts

When both curves shift, the effect on price or quantity may be ambiguous without knowing the relative magnitudes. For example, if demand and supply both increase, quantity definitely rises — but price could rise, fall, or stay the same depending on which shift dominates.

docs.title: Consumer Surplus
docs.text:
Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a good and what they actually pay.

\[\text{Consumer Surplus} = \text{Willingness to Pay} - \text{Price Paid}\]

Graphically, consumer surplus is the area above the price and below the demand curve.

Ticket example

Three fans value a Taylor Swift concert ticket as follows: Fan A: $300, Fan B: $200, Fan C: $100. If tickets sell for $150, only Fan A and Fan B buy. Their consumer surpluses are: - Fan A: $300 − $150 = $150 - Fan B: $200 − $150 = $50 - Total Consumer Surplus = $200

docs.title: Producer Surplus
docs.text:
Producer surplus is the difference between the price producers receive and the minimum price they would have accepted.

\[\text{Producer Surplus} = \text{Price Received} - \text{Minimum Acceptable Price}\]

Graphically, producer surplus is the area below the price and above the supply curve.

docs.title: Total Surplus and Market Efficiency
docs.text:
Total surplus = Consumer surplus + Producer surplus

A competitive market maximizes total surplus — it is allocatively efficient. No reallocation could make someone better off without making someone else worse off (this is Pareto efficiency).

The invisible hand

Adam Smith (1776) observed that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in competitive markets are led by an "invisible hand" to promote the public interest. The supply-and-demand model formalizes this insight: competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Market Any arrangement facilitating exchange between buyers and sellers Demand The relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus Law of Demand As price rises, quantity demanded falls Demand Curve A downward-sloping curve showing quantity demanded at each price Quantity Demanded The specific amount buyers want at a given price Change in Demand A shift of the entire demand curve due to a non-price factor Supply The relationship between price and quantity supplied, ceteris paribus Law of Supply As price rises, quantity supplied rises Supply Curve An upward-sloping curve showing quantity supplied at each price Market Equilibrium The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied Equilibrium Price The market-clearing price (\(P^*\)) Equilibrium Quantity The quantity traded at \(P^*\) Surplus Excess supply when price is above equilibrium Shortage Excess demand when price is below equilibrium Consumer Surplus Difference between willingness to pay and price paid Producer Surplus Difference between price received and minimum acceptable price Total Surplus Consumer surplus + Producer surplus; maximized at competitive equilibrium Normal Good A good for which demand rises as income rises Inferior Good A good for which demand falls as income rises Substitute A good that can replace another; their demands move together Complement A good used with another; their demands move inversely

docs.title: Problem 1 — Shifts in Demand
docs.text:
For each event, state whether demand for the good in bold increases, decreases, or is unchanged. Also state whether this is a movement along the demand curve or a shift.

a) The price of butter rises. What happens to demand for margarine (a substitute)? b) Income rises. What happens to demand for instant ramen noodles (an inferior good)? c) The price of coffee rises. What happens to demand for coffee itself? d) A new study finds that red wine reduces heart disease risk. e) The price of printers falls. What happens to demand for printer ink?

Solution

a) Demand for margarine increases (shifts right) — butter is a substitute; its higher price makes margarine relatively attractive.

b) Demand for instant ramen decreases (shifts left) — inferior good; higher income reduces demand.

c) The quantity demanded of coffee falls (movement along the demand curve) — this is a price change of the good itself, not a shift.

d) Demand for red wine increases (shifts right) — tastes change in favor of the good.

e) Demand for printer ink increases (shifts right) — printers and ink are complements; cheaper printers mean more printers sold, so more ink needed.

docs.title: Problem 2 — Market Equilibrium
docs.text:
The market for apartments in a college town has:

\[Q_d = 1200 - 3P$$ $$Q_s = 300 + 2P\]

where \(Q\) is the number of apartments and \(P\) is monthly rent.

a) Find the equilibrium rent and quantity. b) At a rent of $200/month, is there a surplus or shortage? By how much? c) At a rent of $240/month, is there a surplus or shortage? By how much?

Solution

a) Set \(Q_d = Q_s\):

\[1200 - 3P = 300 + 2P$$ $$900 = 5P$$ $$P^* = \$180, \quad Q^* = 1200 - 3(180) = 660 \text{ apartments}\]

b) At P = $200: - \(Q_d = 1200 - 3(200) = 600\) - \(Q_s = 300 + 2(200) = 700\) - Surplus of 100 apartments (quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded)

c) At P = $240: - \(Q_d = 1200 - 3(240) = 480\) - \(Q_s = 300 + 2(240) = 780\) - Surplus of 300 apartments

docs.title: Problem 3 — Equilibrium Changes
docs.text:
In the market for gasoline, explain the effect on the equilibrium price and quantity of each event. State clearly which curve shifts, in which direction, and what happens to \(P^*\) and \(Q^*\).

a) The price of crude oil (a key input) rises sharply. b) Higher fuel efficiency standards cause consumers to drive less. c) A new refinery opens, and simultaneously, the price of electric vehicles falls (reducing demand for gasoline).

Solution

a) Supply decreases (shifts left) — higher input cost. - \(P^*\) rises, \(Q^*\) falls.

b) Demand decreases (shifts left) — consumers want less gasoline at every price. - \(P^*\) falls, \(Q^*\) falls.

c) Supply increases (new refinery → shifts right) AND Demand decreases (cheaper EVs reduce gas demand → shifts left). - Both shifts push \(Q^*\) down (unambiguously). - Effect on \(P^*\) is ambiguous — supply increase pushes price down, demand decrease also pushes price down, so \(P^*\) falls (in this case both effects reinforce each other).

docs.title: Problem 4 — Consumer and Producer Surplus
docs.text:
The supply and demand for a good are:

\[Q_d = 80 - P$$ $$Q_s = 20 + P\]

a) Find equilibrium P* and Q*. b) Calculate consumer surplus at equilibrium. c) Calculate producer surplus at equilibrium. d) What is total surplus?

Solution

a) Set \(Q_d = Q_s\): \(80 - P = 20 + P \Rightarrow 60 = 2P \Rightarrow P^* = 30, \; Q^* = 50\)

b) Consumer surplus is the area of the triangle above the price and below the demand curve.

The demand curve hits the vertical axis when \(Q_d = 0\): \(0 = 80 - P \Rightarrow P = 80\).

\[\text{CS} = \frac{1}{2} \times (80 - 30) \times 50 = \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 50 = \$1{,}250\]

c) Producer surplus is the area of the triangle below the price and above the supply curve.

The supply curve hits the vertical axis when \(Q_s = 0\): \(0 = 20 + P \Rightarrow P = -20\). Wait — the supply curve starts where \(Q_s = 0\), so: \(20 + P = 0 \Rightarrow P = -20\). But negative prices don't make sense here. The minimum supply price (the y-intercept of supply when we solve for P) is: the supply curve starts supplying when price is such that \(Q_s > 0\), i.e., when \(P > -20\). At \(P = 0\), \(Q_s = 20\).

More precisely: solving \(Q_s = 20 + P\) for P: \(P = Q_s - 20\). The supply curve (as \(P\) as a function of \(Q\)) is \(P = Q - 20\). It intercepts the horizontal axis (P=0) at Q=20, and the P-axis at P=-20. Since we can't have negative prices in this market context, the supply curve effectively starts at Q=20 when P=0.

Producer surplus = area below P* = 30 and above the supply curve, from Q=0 to Q=50. Since the supply "curve" P = Q - 20 intersects P=0 at Q=20 and P=30 at Q=50:

\[\text{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \times (30 - (-20)) \times 50 = \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 50 = \$1{,}250\]

Alternatively, using the triangular area with base 50 (from Q=0 to Q=50) and height = 30 - (-20) = 50: PS = ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

d) Total surplus = CS + PS = $1,250 + $1,250 = $2,500.

docs.title: Problem 5 — Real World Application
docs.text:
In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic caused the demand for hand sanitizer to increase dramatically. At the same time, some producers switched from producing other goods to producing hand sanitizer (supply increased).

a) What happened to the equilibrium quantity of hand sanitizer? Explain. b) Is the effect on equilibrium price certain or ambiguous? Explain. c) During the pandemic, many stores ran out of hand sanitizer despite producers ramping up. Is this consistent with the supply-and-demand model? What does it suggest about prices?

Solution

a) Equilibrium quantity definitely increased — both the demand increase and the supply increase push quantity upward. The two effects reinforce each other.

b) The effect on price is ambiguous. The demand increase pushes price up; the supply increase pushes price down. The net effect depends on which shift was larger.

c) Running out of stock is a shortage — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price. This is consistent with supply-and-demand theory when price is held below equilibrium. Many retailers chose not to raise prices (for ethical or reputational reasons), so prices did not rise to clear the market. This suggests that the equilibrium price for hand sanitizer rose substantially — but price controls (informal or formal) prevented prices from reaching equilibrium.

Next Chapter

In Chapter 3: Elasticity, we measure how much quantity demanded and supplied respond to price changes — a crucial tool for business and policy analysis.

docs.title: About This Section
docs.text: This section provides curated AI prompts you can use with Claude or other large language models to deepen your understanding of microeconomics. The prompts are organized by chapter and learning objective.

docs.title: How to Use These Prompts
docs.text:
1. Open Claude (or your preferred AI assistant) in a new tab.
  2. Copy and paste a prompt below.
  3. Read the response critically — AI can make mistakes. Use your textbook and lecture notes to verify.
  4. Follow up with your own questions to dig deeper.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Microeconomics
docs.text:
• "Explain the concept of opportunity cost using an example from my daily life as a college student."
  • "What is the difference between a movement along a PPF and a shift of the PPF? Give a real-world example of each."
  • "Give me three examples of sunk cost fallacies from business history."

docs.title: Chapter 2: Supply and Demand
docs.text:
• "Walk me through how to find market equilibrium algebraically, step by step."
  • "What happens to the equilibrium price and quantity in the market for coffee if both the price of coffee beans rises and a health study finds coffee reduces cancer risk? Which effect dominates?"
  • "Explain why a price ceiling below equilibrium causes a shortage, using a concrete example like rent control."

docs.title: Chapter 10: Game Theory
docs.text:
• "Explain the prisoner's dilemma to me as if I've never studied economics. Then explain why it is relevant to oligopoly markets."
  • "What is a Nash equilibrium, and why is it not always the best outcome for society?"

More prompts will be added as chapters are completed. Contributions welcome via GitHub.

docs.title: About MicroSims
docs.text: MicroSims are interactive, browser-based simulations that let you explore microeconomic models by changing parameters and observing how the model responds. No installation required.

docs.title: Planned Simulations
docs.text:
Simulation Chapter Description Production Possibilities Frontier Ch. 1 Adjust resources and technology; see how the PPF shifts Supply & Demand Ch. 2 Shift supply and demand curves; observe equilibrium changes Elasticity Explorer Ch. 3 Change elasticity; see how total revenue responds to price changes Budget Constraint Ch. 4 Adjust income and prices; find consumer optimum Cost Curves Ch. 5 See how fixed/variable costs shape ATC, AVC, MC Competitive Market Ch. 6 Entry and exit in the long run Monopoly Pricing Ch. 7 Set price or quantity; see deadweight loss Prisoner's Dilemma Ch. 10 Play strategic games against an AI opponent Externality Ch. 13 Compare private vs. social optimum; apply a Pigouvian tax Nudge Lab Ch. 15 Design choice architectures and see how behavior changes

Simulations are built using Python (Panel/Bokeh) or JavaScript (Observable Plot). Source code will be available in the GitHub repository.
